posts.text:
**Song of Solomon 1**
*1  The song of songs, which is Solomon’s.*

*2  Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: for thy love is better than wine.*

*3  Because of the savour of thy good ointments thy name is as ointment poured forth, therefore do the virgins love thee.*

*4  Draw me, we will run after thee: the king hath brought me into his chambers: we will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.*

*5  I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon.*

*6  Look not upon me, because I am black, because the sun hath looked upon me: my mother’s children were angry with me; they made me the keeper of the vineyards; but mine own vineyard have I not kept.*

*7  Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou makest thy flock to rest at noon: for why should I be as one that turneth aside by the flocks of thy companions?*

*8  If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents.*

*9  I have compared thee, O my love, to a company of horses in Pharaoh’s chariots.*

*10  Thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels, thy neck with chains of gold.*

*11  We will make thee borders of gold with studs of silver.*

*12  While the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof.*

*13  A bundle of myrrh is my well-beloved unto me; he shall lie all night betwixt my breasts.*

*14  My beloved is unto me as a cluster of camphire in the vineyards of Engedi.*

*15  Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes.*

*16  Behold, thou art fair, my beloved, yea, pleasant: also our bed is green.*

*17  The beams of our house are cedar, and our rafters of fir.*

We are in the penultimate book of the Bible for the purposes of my goal to write out studies of every book of the Bible. Only Song of Songs and Psalms remain.

Here in the first chapter of Solomon's ode to his love, we can observe why it is in scripture; the clear allegory of Christ and His beloved, the saved.

The poetic language used, going back and forth between the woman and the man, is beautiful prose in itself. Begging for kisses from one whose love is better than wine. Whose savour is as good ointments.

The use of ointment and fine, perfumed oils as a representation of the Spirit, is found throughout the Bible. Her saying that even the king's name is as an ointment poured forth, that the virgins, or the innocent ladies in wait, do love him. Just as the righteous in Christ love even the name of Jesus.

She says to draw them, the damsels, to call them. And they will run after him. Just as the Spirit calls us, as a sweet savour to those that seek Him, calls us, and we willingly respond. *We will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.*

The upright, like virgin, indicates the quality of the saved. We are the righteousness of God. We have Jesus imputed righteousness upon us and a new man within, making us as virgins in His eyes. The forgiveness of the Father. We are upright because He is upright, and we are His.

 *I am black, but comely*...the woman isn't referring to race here, but the darkness of her skin from the sun. Her mother's children were angry with her, forcing her to keep their vineyards and to feed the sheep.

But the blackness is also sin, what it does to our heart. And the daughters are unbelieving Israel. They who persecuted the prophets and would crucify Christ. The world hates believers, because of His love for us. That despite our sin and being made their servants to do the work of the field, He so loves us.

The bride, having spoken of her love, and having told the daughters of Jerusalem her unworthiness, and having sought to find the king, hears back from him.

She seeks out his flocks, to be with him, and Solomon responds to her in verse 8. *If thou know not, O thou fairest among women, go thy way forth by the footsteps of the flock, and feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents.*

He praises her, after her own shameful confession. She calls herself black from the work of being a servant. He calls her most fair among women. This is how Christ views His own.

Solomon says, follow the footsteps of the flock. Find the shepherds. We are Jesus' sheep. He is our Good Shepherd. We may find Him where the other sheep are, and follow in their footsteps that we may know Him.

Solomon goes on to describe his beloved in epic terms, and the chorus of the daughters of Jerusalem tells of how they will dress her in fine jewels and ornaments of fine gold and silver as the King's desire. Where before the children of Israel had despised her, the fair daughters of Jerusalem follow the lead of the King, and honor who he has chosen.

Verse 12 sees the woman at the King's table. In his court. The spiced wine calls him. She compares her attraction to him as the pleasant smell of myrrh, and her desire is for him to lay upon her bosom all night.

He is like a cluster of henna flowers, or *camphire*, alluring, heavily scented clusters of small white and yellow flowers used as perfume.

She longs for him, his eyes like a doves. Their bed green. The beams cedar and rafters fir. The finest materials build their house, and she wishes to live with him forever.

**Song of Solomon 2**
*1  I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.*

*2  As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters.*

*3  As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.*

*4  He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.*

*5  Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.*

*6  His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me.*

*7  I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.*

*8  The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills.*

*9  My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, shewing himself through the lattice.*

*10  My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away.*

*11  For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone;*

*12  The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land;*

*13  The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give a good smell. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away.*

*14  O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.*

*15  Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.*

*16  My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.*

*17  Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether*.

Chapter 2 contains a poetic back and forth dialogue between the woman and the man, the rose of Sharon and her beloved, an apple tree among the trees of the wood. He compares other women to thorns, but she is a lily, a beautiful flower among them.

The woman delights in his shade, his protection, and in his fruit, which is sweet to her taste. He calls her to his banquet, under the banner of love.

Again, we see the gospel. He is the tree of life, over a precious flower among the thorns. Invited to the banquet house of the Lord. The wedding supper of the Lamb.

She is overcome by his love, she longs for him as we long for Jesus, and His embrace in that great day of redemption.

 *I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.*

The timing of the Lord's return is at God's pleasure. Just as she waits for her love to awake, we patiently wait for Him to return.

The roes, the hinds of the field are the wild deer that play in the pastures and roam the hills and mountains.

She hears the voice of her beloved, and compares him to the roebuck leaping and skipping on mountains and hills. She sees him through the lattice of the window, just beyond her walls, and he speaks to her, calling her to rise up and come with him.

This pictures the return of Christ, gathering the elect from the four corners of the world. Jesus descends with a shout. We who are His hear His voice, and Rise up, and come away with Him.

*For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone;* it is spring. The rains fall and the flowers burst forth, and a time of peace is at hand. The signs of the season are showing. The fig tree puts forth her green figs.

**Matthew 24:32–33**
*Now learn a parable of the fig tree; When his branch is yet tender, and putteth forth leaves, ye know that summer is nigh: So likewise ye, when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near, even at the doors.*

She begs to see her love, he is among the clefts of the rock, the stairs of the mountains, as a dove, his face is upon those that take shelter from His wrath there. They fear him. But she longs to see him.

**Revelation 6:15–17**
*And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every bondman, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains; And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?*

*Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines have tender grapes.* The wrath is upon these "little foxes," the wicked, those that spoil and corrupt the tender grapes. The wicked that seek to destroy the believers, especially during the great tribulation.

Her certainty of their love, that he is hers and she is his, even as he waits for his time, reflects the eternal security we have as believers in Christ. Waiting patiently for His return, when the day breaks and the shadows flee the light.

**Song of Solomon 3**
*1  By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.*

*2  I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.*

*3  The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?*

*4  It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.*

*5  I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please.*

*6  Who is this that cometh out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all powders of the merchant?*

*7  Behold his bed, which is Solomon’s; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel.*

*8  They all hold swords, being expert in war: every man hath his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night.*

*9  King Solomon made himself a chariot of the wood of Lebanon.*

*10  He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.*

*11  Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart.*

Chapter 3 begins with the woman waking to a desolate bed, unable to find her beloved. Seeking him, she desperately searches in the night, throughout the city streets. She repeats the refrain that she *sought him, but I found him not.*

She then encounters the night watch, and enquires of them if they had seen *him, whom my soul loveth.*

This passage beautifully reflects the death of Christ, picturing the panicked feeling of believers at His death, and at the empty tomb. The watchmen, the religious leaders who crucified Him, unable to give an answer, but then, in her search, she finds him. *Him whom my soul loveth.*

And she holds him and will not let him go, bringing him into her mother's house, even to the bed chamber she was conceived in. As Jesus comes into us, and is held in the most intimate chamber of our hearts.

For the second time in the song, the chorus in verse 5, also found in chapter 2:7 is repeated:

*I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, till he please*.

It is repeated again in chapter 8, and the verse is used as transition in the structure of the song.

While it may picture the current time, where we wait for our beloved, the Lord Jesus to return, it also serves as an oath, asking the daughters of Jerusalem to swear by the roes and hinds, the graceful and skittish deer of the land, to not stir the Beloved too early. To let him sleep as late as he pleases.

The immediate application speaks to the delicate nature of love, especially in its earliest stages, where you almost feel a surreal and magical experience and are afraid it could burst like a bubble at any time. You don't want to lose that joyous state. You don't want it to be disturbed, like the gazelles of the mountains startled at a sudden movement or sound.

She has found her beloved and taken him into her heart, and wants that joy of her salvation to last.

The chorus serves to transition the narrative to an epic description of the King, and his entourage, emerging from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, an endless caravan. Perfumed and decked out in fine clothes for the wedding.

This pictures the return of Christ, after the wrath, on a white horse with ten thousands of His saints, wearing their wedding clothes, prepared for the marriage supper of the Lamb.

The bed of the King, his chariot, surrounded by threescore valiant men, the valiant of Israel. The soldiers with swords at their hip, like the prophets armed with the word of God.

King Solomon's chariot, made of the finest wood, decked in silver and gold, covered in royal purple, and as it goes, *paved with love*, *for the daughters of Jerusalem*. This is the interior of the royal chariot, embroidery made by the daughters of the land with love, the inner bed, where the King and his bride would recline.

The purity of God in the silver pillars, His grace, the gold that surrounds us. The purple of His majesty as Lord, and the interior, the soft comfort of His love for us.

The bride of the song calls out for the daughters of Zion, Jerusalem, to go out and welcome the King. To examine his wedding crown, to celebrate the betrothal and his gladness. The tradition of the people is that the mother of the bridegroom crafts a crown to celebrate the nuptials. Not a crown of royalty, but of love.

In **Revelation 19:12**, as Christ rides forth to claim ultimate victory and gather His people, the text says, *on his head were many crowns*.

The crowns of Christ at His triumphant arrival to meet the descending New Jerusalem, adorned as a bride, are the diadem of His love for His beloved, just as Solomon's love for his bride.

As John writes in *Revelation 21:2*:
*And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.*

The allegory and picture of the King of Kings arriving at His wedding feast, at the culmination of history, to usher in His millennial Kingdom, reflected in the prophetic love song written by Solomon.

**Song of Solomon 4**
*1  Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; thou hast doves’ eyes within thy locks: thy hair is as a flock of goats, that appear from mount Gilead.*

*2  Thy teeth are like a flock of sheep that are even shorn, which came up from the washing; whereof every one bear twins, and none is barren among them.*

*3  Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks.*

*4  Thy neck is like the tower of David builded for an armoury, whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, all shields of mighty men.*

*5  Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins, which feed among the lilies.*

*6  Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, I will get me to the mountain of myrrh, and to the hill of frankincense.*

*7  Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.*

*8  Come with me from Lebanon, my spouse, with me from Lebanon: look from the top of Amana, from the top of Shenir and Hermon, from the lions’ dens, from the mountains of the leopards.*

*9  Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.*

*10  How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse! how much better is thy love than wine! and the smell of thine ointments than all spices!*

*11  Thy lips, O my spouse, drop as the honeycomb: honey and milk are under thy tongue; and the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon.*

*12  A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.*

*13  Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,*

*14  Spikenard and saffron; calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief spices:*

*15  A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon.*

*16  Awake, O north wind; and come, thou south; blow upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flow out. Let my beloved come into his garden, and eat his pleasant fruits.*

Chapter 4 opens with an ode to the beloved bride by her lover, the bridegroom. When he looks upon her he sees her fair beauty, her eyes as doves', her hair as the flocks of wild mountain goats. Picturing her black, flowing locks as the long, black, silky hair the goats have. When a herd of these dark goats grazes and moves down a steep mountain from a distance, the flowing movement creates a visual illusion of cascading hair.

He compares her teeth to the whitest of sheep, shorn and clean and notes there are none missing, a rarity to be sure in the ancient world.

Her lips, red as scarlet thread and her speech comely. Her temples and neck and breasts and scent, perfect and without blemish.

*Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee.*

The poetic nature of the song, romanticizing the couples love, could be seen as hyperbole. The aura of beauty that comes with infatuation. The perfection we see when we are caught up in our love for the other.

But, as a spiritual allegory, we see the woman, who works the field and vineyard, black skinned, is without blemish when the King looks upon her. Just as we who are saved and sanctified by faith in Christ are pure when the Lord looks upon us. Clothed in righteousness. No sin imputed upon our new man.

**2 Corinthians 5:21**
*For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.*

He has made us without blemish;

**Colossians 1:21–22**
*And you, that were sometime alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked works, yet now hath he reconciled In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight*

Solomon's King sings passionately about his beloved; *How fair is thy love, my sister, my spouse!* A sister of Israel, his spouse through their betrothal and marriage.

This is also how Jesus sees us, His beloved. We are His brothers and sisters, and spouse as a collective. Made one within the body of Christ.

**Matthew 12:50**
*For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother*.

His idealized view of us, despite our sin and despite our falling short of the glory of God, comes entirely by His love for us. That while we were sinners, Christ died for us. That He justifies the ungodly. That the Spirit quickens and seals us unto redemption.

So when Solomon compares his love to an inclosed garden, walled off, a spring shut up, barred from use by others. A fountain sealed, carrying the seal of the King, and so kept pure from pollution. In this allegory we see the promise of eternal security in Christ. We are eternally His.

The fruits of the garden are orchards, even pomegranates, and pleasant fruits, and flowers and spices used in ointments and perfume. Spikenard, the precious Himalayan plant, used to anoint Christ;

**Mark 14:3**
*And being in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at meat, there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head.*

The odors of her garden are pleasing. Precious to the King.  Just as our fruit, our good works in Christ, are pleasing to Him.

*A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, and streams from Lebanon*. He views us and the works we do for Him the same way, and we issue forth the living waters of the Spirit when we walk in His ways.

The chapter ends shifting to the beloved woman, the bride, calling upon her lord to enter her garden, *that the spices thereof may flow out.* Spiritually, calling upon the name of the Lord, that one may be saved, that God may eat His pleasant fruits.

**Song of Solomon 5**
*1  I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.*

*2  I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night.*

*3  I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?*

*4  My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him.*

*5  I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock.*

*6  I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.*

*7  The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me.*

*8  I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.*

*9  What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?*

*10  My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand.*

*11  His head is as the most fine gold, his locks are bushy, and black as a raven.*

*12  His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, and fitly set.*

*13  His cheeks are as a bed of spices, as sweet flowers: his lips like lilies, dropping sweet smelling myrrh.*

*14  His hands are as gold rings set with the beryl: his belly is as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires.*

*15  His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.*

*16  His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.*

Chapter 5 opens with the aftermath of the close of the previous chapter, which ended with the woman calling upon her bridegroom, her lord.

The spiritual moment of acceptance and humility, asking Him for salvation. Opening yourself to be intimately known of God.

Verse 1 gives the bridegroom's POV. Having entered the garden, come unto his dearest sister, his spouse, gathered the spices and ointments of myrrh, eaten the sweet of the honeycomb, drunk the wine and milk, and calling those at the wedding feast, and his bride, to eat and drink, abundantly.

**Revelation 22:17**
*And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.*

This picture of salvation, the immediate joy and celebration, the call to get your fill of an abundance of the sweet and precious food and anointing oils, wine and milk, to drink abundantly, is God's call to us to now walk in His Spirit. To take full advantage of the relationship His children have with the Father in Christ, the true King. The Shepherd. The Bridegroom. Not a thief, but our Savior.

**John 10:10**
*The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.*

We are called to walk in the Spirit and receive the fruit thereof;

**Galatians 5:22–25**
*But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.*

This initial feeling of having come to a feast and being overwhelmed with the love of God towards us, His blessings and rest, is marvelous. But we may tire and sleep in that contentment.

The bride sleeps, but her heart wakes. She hears a knock. A voice. It is her beloved, calling to her to let him in. He asks her to open to him, *my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled*. He has come, his hair wet with the dew of the night to see her.

He is Christ come to give His bride a blessing, but she doesn't leap to open the door.

She makes excuses; *I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?* Rather than hear His voice and do His will, that we may be blessed, a believer may see their contentment and undefiled spirit as a bed to rest upon. When God asks so little of us whom He has saved, to open when He knocks, will we respond?

**Revelation 3:20**
*Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.*

In the Christian life, God gives us works to do. Poor to be fed. A gospel to be preached. Divine appointments to be kept. His burden is light. He wants so little from us, yet in our own selfish interests, we make excuses. Taking for granted all He has given us.

And, even as the beloved reaches his hand in through the door, making that extra effort to stir his bride, God will try and overcome our hesitation, moving in our lives.

His effort stirs her. She rises but too late. She feels the sweet smelling myrrh, the holiness of Christ, upon the lock. But, He has withdrawn.

When we don't respond to God's callings, and hesitate to do His will, He will give us a taste of life without Him. He will lift His hedge of protection. He will let us suffer consequences He has spared us from. He will chasten every son.

The bride's soul fails, knowing she did wrong and desperately she seeks her beloved, in the very manner she once sought him. Wandering in the dark streets, calling for him. Trying to find her own way.

This time, the watchmen find her and persecute her. The smote her and wound her and remove her veil of purity. She suffers for her love's sake.

The watchmen who could not tell her the way to her love in chapter 3, now treat her wickedly.

This could be false teachers, those religious leaders who were not able to give her the gospel, now kicking her when she's down, to try and spoil her faith.

We may backslide. We may become complacent. We may try to avoid doing His work. We may ignore His calling and then, when tribulation comes, look for Him where He is not, seeking answers. And we may be subject to tribulation, to remind us that we need Him, to remind us we are His.

Just as Jonah was brought to Nineveh in the whale. Just as the church in Jerusalem, ordained to spread the gospel to the four corners of the world, stayed in Judea until the persecution against them scattered many. Just like Paul's repeated attempts to win his countrymen led him again and again to Jerusalem, finally being brought out and delivered to Rome in chains.

It's hard to kick against the pricks.

And so beaten and bloody, the bride charges an oath to the daughters of Jerusalem; *if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.*

To our modern years this sounds bad, but what's being said is that she is sick from love, overwhelmed by her feelings. Lovesick for her beloved.

Despite persecution, she will not renounce him. Despite tribulation for his sake, she still longs for him. And she tells others who may be seeking him to give him her message of love.

The daughters of Jerusalem answer her refrain;

*What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us?*

She has been backslidden, treated horribly by the authorities, bloody, aiming to destroy her remaining faith and strip away her public testimony (the veil), and yet her love is true.

The daughters cannot understand what makes her beloved so special, above all others, that she would still call to him after all she's suffered.

Unsaved people who see Christians suffer for Christ and still preach His love, often are baffled, but sometimes are moved. When the churches have been persecuted, traditionally we have seen exponential growth. Men are persuaded to willingly go to their death for the cause of Christ, and this testimony brings others to the faith.

Why is your beloved more than others? Why is your God over the gods of men?

And she answers.

He is white, with purity, sinless. Divine. Ruddy, a red complexion picturing the humanity of Jesus and blood shed for us. The chiefest among ten those, the Lord of hosts. King of kings.

Crowned of gold, sovereign above all. His locks, eternally young, everlasting. His eyes, full of grace and compassion for His beloved.

Kissing His cheeks, like a bed of spices. Sweet flowers. His kiss, soft like the petals of the lily, dripping with precious oils. His love and our love for Him.

The strength of His hands, the purity of His works, the gold and precious stones of all that He does. The inward parts of Christ are strong and pure as ivory, with heavenly blue sapphires the eternal Godhead in Him.

His legs, a picture of Jesus' unmoving and unswerving strength. He supports us and His ways are golden. Pure. His face, chiseled as the great cedars. His mouth is sweet, all that He says is true.

*This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem*. Oh what a friend we have in Jesus!

**Song of Solomon 6**
*1  Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women? whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee.*

*2  My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.*

*3  I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilies.*

*4  Thou art beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army with banners.*

*5  Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me: thy hair is as a flock of goats that appear from Gilead.*

*6  Thy teeth are as a flock of sheep which go up from the washing, whereof every one beareth twins, and there is not one barren among them.*

*7  As a piece of a pomegranate are thy temples within thy locks.*

*8  There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number.*

*9  My dove, my undefiled is but one; she is the only one of her mother, she is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her; yea, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her.*

*10  Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?*

*11  I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, and to see whether the vine flourished, and the pomegranates budded.*

*12  Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Amminadib.*

*13  Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies.*

The daughters of Jerusalem chorus in chapter 5 asked of the woman; *What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women?*

The chapter ends with the woman, battered and bloody from the world's treatment of her for his sake, extolling his virtues and singing praise to his perfection.

The character arc from the ecstatic bride at the feast to the complacent woman, making excuses to avoid her love, then realizing and searching him out again, only to be mistreated by the watchmen and questioned by the daughters, and ultimately to still profess her love and devotion for Jesus, is a wonderful picture of things that can and do happen in the Christian life.

And her faith through the trials leads others to seek Him.

Chapter 6 opens with the same chorus of daughters, and they have changed their tune.

*Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women? whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee.*

Our testimony, especially in persecution, not only reestablishes our faith, but leads others to seek Jesus.

We can often feel adrift. We may realize we should do more for the cause of Christ. We may have a sense of separation from Him. We may call out in prayer as David did:

**Psalms 51:12**
*Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.*

But we should be aware that as saved Christians, seeking to get back on the right path, we will see persecution. The devil will attempt to sift us like wheat. Satan doesn't need much to keep the unsaved from seeking truth, but he works overtime to keep Christians from being fruitful.

So, having persuaded the daughters, the woman answers them; that she knows where her beloved has gone. He is down in His garden, to feed the garden and gather lilies. A picture of the gospel light, the harvest of believers, the fruit of His good pleasure.

She affirms her faith; *I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: he feedeth among the lilie*s, and then the narrator shifts again to the King.

He praises his beloved, comparing her beauty to Tirzah, a city known for its natural beauty, and even as Jerusalem, ready for war, filled with bannermen, armies ready to march.

He is overwhelmed with her beauty, repeating the verses poetically comparing her hair and teeth to goats and sheep as the lyrics from chapter 4.

He numbers her among 60 queens and 80 concubines and countless virgins, a royal harem, and says she alone is above them all. Undefiled. The choice daughter, whom all the other women blessed and praised. Beloved above them all.

Verse 10, the daughters of Jerusalem, the very courtesans the King compared his beloved to, sing her praises.

*Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?*

We are His beloved. We are the light of the world. We shine forth to all nations, calling them to Christ. Provoking them to envy, that they may seek to be His bride.

The woman sings in verse 11, that she has gone down to her beloved's garden. To see the fruit of the garden, and if the vine flourished, Jesus is the true vine. She's returned to His rest, as quickly as the chariots, to her beloved, upon seeing the bounty of his garden.

The daughters encourage her, *Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee.* And her beloved asks them *What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies.* A refrain answered in the next chapter.

It is worth noting that the woman of the Song of Solomon is often referred to as the "*Shulamite* Woman" based on verse 13.

There are conflicting theories as to what that means; is it a region, a nation, a family name? Some believe it is a feminine form of Solomon. The evidence for any of these ideas is scant, and I have purposefully refrained from calling the woman a Shulamite because, in my opinion, in the end it doesn't matter to understand the context and subtext of the Song.

You may disagree, and that's ok.

**Song of Solomon 7**
*1  How beautiful are thy feet with shoes, O prince’s daughter! the joints of thy thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a cunning workman.*

*2  Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies.*

*3  Thy two breasts are like two young roes that are twins.*

*4  Thy neck is as a tower of ivory; thine eyes like the fishpools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bathrabbim: thy nose is as the tower of Lebanon which looketh toward Damascus.*

*5  Thine head upon thee is like Carmel, and the hair of thine head like purple; the king is held in the galleries.*

*6  How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!*

*7  This thy stature is like to a palm tree, and thy breasts to clusters of grapes.*

*8  I said, I will go up to the palm tree, I will take hold of the boughs thereof: now also thy breasts shall be as clusters of the vine, and the smell of thy nose like apples;*

*9  And the roof of thy mouth like the best wine for my beloved, that goeth down sweetly, causing the lips of those that are asleep to speak.*

*10  I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me.*

*11  Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; let us lodge in the villages.*

*12  Let us get up early to the vineyards; let us see if the vine flourish, whether the tender grape appear, and the pomegranates bud forth: there will I give thee my loves.*

*13  The mandrakes give a smell, and at our gates are all manner of pleasant fruits, new and old, which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved.*

Song of Solomon 7 opens with the King, having called his beloved Shulamite woman to return to him that he may look upon her at the end of chapter 6, now detailing what he sees of his beloved. He describes her beauty and the perfect symmetry of her body.

*How fair and how pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!*

Everything he sees of her is good. Just as we are seen as perfect and without spot when God looks upon us, clothed in the righteousness of Christ.

**2 Corinthians 11:2**
*For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.*

**Colossians 1:22**
*In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight*

**Jude 1:24–25**
*Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, To the only wise God our Saviour, be glory and majesty, dominion and power, both now and ever. Amen.*

The woman responds to her husband, her brother, her spouse with unwavering confidence;

*I am my beloved’s, and his desire is toward me.*

We are Christ's, and His desire is for us.

Beginning there in verse 10, she responds to her beloved, knowing she is his, and inviting him to go forth with her, to live with her. To get up early to the vineyards, to see the vine flourish and come to fruition, where she will give him her love.

The spiritual application here; She has gone from her initial humble acceptance of his love, to the joy of the wedding feast, to her period of complacency, persecution, profession of faith and renewal, to now making the decision to plan her day and life around him, is a beautiful picture of the Christian life.

A believer makes the conscious decision to make Jesus their companion. To go forth with Him and to reside with Him. To wake early in the morning, starting the day with Christ, and His word. In prayer.

This intentionality is contrasted with the bride laying in bed, hesitant to wake, making excuses to avoid letting in her beloved. As mature Christians, in it for the long haul, we seek Him first.

We work with Him to tend the vine, which is His church, bringing forth fruit which are new believers. Planting the seed of His word. Watering and nurturing. Tending to them, the babes in Christ, and helping them grow to maturity. Through it all, giving Him all our love.

We lay up our fruit, those people we have given the gospel to, the needy to whom we give comfort. The broken hearted we have consoled. This treasure we have laid up for Heaven, but to Him is the increase. We give Him our all because He is our beloved.

**Song of Solomon 8**
*1  O that thou wert as my brother, that sucked the breasts of my mother! when I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; yea, I should not be despised.*

*2  I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother’s house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate.*

*3  His left hand should be under my head, and his right hand should embrace me.*

*4  I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.*

*5  Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved? I raised thee up under the apple tree: there thy mother brought thee forth: there she brought thee forth that bare thee.*

*6  Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.*

*7  Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.*

*8  We have a little sister, and she hath no breasts: what shall we do for our sister in the day when she shall be spoken for?*

*9  If she be a wall, we will build upon her a palace of silver: and if she be a door, we will inclose her with boards of cedar.*

*10  I am a wall, and my breasts like towers: then was I in his eyes as one that found favour.*

*11  Solomon had a vineyard at Baalhamon; he let out the vineyard unto keepers; every one for the fruit thereof was to bring a thousand pieces of silver.*

*12  My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred.*

*13  Thou that dwellest in the gardens, the companions hearken to thy voice: cause me to hear it.*

*14  Make haste, my beloved, and be thou like to a roe or to a young hart upon the mountains of spices.*

We are in the final chapter of the Song of Solomon, and the opening verses are the woman, longing to openly display affection for her beloved, the way a sister and brother as family could, without being despised. Without the judgment that would come for a maiden to kiss and embrace a lover, even betrothed, in public.

We seem to have come full circle to the beginning of the song. The wedding hasn't happened, the separation and then regained relationship. It is as if she's been dreaming the experience from courtship to maturity, as told in chapters 2-7.

There are repeated stanzas, ideas and the chorus again in verse 4;

 *I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that ye stir not up, nor awake my love, until he please.*

The longing to be with him, and to experience his love, to be in his embrace, echos her plaintive desires in the first few chapters.

But here, after charging the daughters of Jerusalem again, they sing;

*Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?*

They see the love-changed woman, who was the girl they had watched grow.

The woman professes her love;

*Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm: for love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.*

The eternal and unbreakable seal of the Spirit, set upon our hearts, once we know Him and are known of Him.

The love of Christ is like an unquenchable fire, the floods cannot drown it. Noah found grace in the eyes of God. His love for man endured, despite *the* flood.

The love of God could not be purchased, even if a rich man sold all his substance for love, he would be despised. It is not found in riches and cannot be bought by our works. It is unmerited. Freely given.

The woman's brothers join the choir, seeing their sister still as the immature girl they have known. Wondering what they shall do for her now, at her betrothal. A reality that big brothers and parents face, when their daughter has matured.

They contemplate what they'd do metaphorically, if she were a foundational wall or a door in need of a frame. But she states that she is fully grown. She is a wall and the breasts of her maturity are towers. An allegory for the maturity to come to the Lord, and find His grace.

Then a parable of her beloved, the lord Solomon, and his vineyard. He let, or leased it out to keepers, to be dressed. And their charge was a thousand pieces of silver, purchased by the fruit they would harvest.

The same is the vineyards of Christ's parables. The talents of silver. The harvest and the increase. The unprofitable servants of Israel, the wicked keepers who slew the prophets and even the Son of the Lord. The spiritual understanding that comes from knowing this first; the Lord planted a vineyard;

**Isaiah 5:1–7**
*Now will I sing to my wellbeloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard. My wellbeloved hath a vineyard in a very fruitful hill: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes. And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down: And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.*

The woman offers her vineyard to Solomon, pledging the tribute of a thousand, and even the keepers, a wage of two hundred. Pledging her fruit to her Lord.

The Lord planted and cultivated a vineyard with Israel, and the husband men betrayed Him. But the woman, as the faithful believer willingly offers herself as a vineyard, and freely gives the Lord His tribute. The fruit we gather. The works we do for the cause of the gospel. She gladly pays the workers a wage. Just as we do with tithes and offerings to sustain our pastors, our churches, ministries and missionaries, that work in the fields for God.

The Song of Solomon ends with prayer. She calls upon the Lord, acknowledging that the companions of God hear His voice. His sheep. She asks, humbly, to hear His voice as He calls.

We should always listen for that still, small voice. We should pray that God gives us ears to hear His will.

Her final prayer is that her love come quickly. To make haste in His return, to come down upon the mountains, as a roe or young hart, gazelle among the spices.

The prayer for *Thy Kingdom, come.* Or *Even so, come, Lord Jesus,* is found throughout scripture. *Maranatha,* come quickly.

**2 Peter 3:12**
*Looking for and hastening unto the coming of the day of God, wherein the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat?*

This is our hope, for the day of the Lord. His gathering of His people, the resurrection of the saints into glory. His terrible and fearful wrath on the ungodly.

As mature Christians, we should be as the woman, gladly giving ourselves to the Lord, and praying to hear His voice, praying for His return. She has come to understand love, through Him. And has gladly given herself to Him.

The spiritual journey that the believer takes, is beautifully captured in the Song of Solomon. From the first glimpse of love, to the calling upon the Lord, the ups and downs, and final devotional surrender, is breathtaking in its beauty and the prophetic power of the song.

Believers are His beloved. When, in verse 5, the daughters of Jerusalem sing *Who is this that cometh up from the wilderness, leaning upon her beloved?* It is such a fitting picture of our salvation. How the believer emerges from the wilderness, not walking on her own strength, but "*leaning upon her beloved*." She is changed, sealed by the Holy Spirit. Eternally His.

Amen.
